units.name: command-core
units.role: Define what a CLI command is, organize commands into a tree, dispatch the one the user typed, and render its help/usage/version text.
units.description: This is the heart of the library: it defines what a 'command' is (a name, a description, some flags, and the function that runs when it is invoked), how commands nest into a parent/child tree so things like 'git remote add' work the way people expect, how the right command gets picked out of what the user typed, and how help, usage, and version text get printed. Every other piece of this library — argument checking, flag-grouping rules, shell tab-completion, and documentation generation — is built on top of the command object defined here.

units.name: arg-validators
units.role: Ready-made policies for checking whether the user supplied the right positional arguments.
units.description: This is the library of rules a command-line tool uses to check whether the user typed the right number, or kind, of extra words after a command — for example 'mytool copy SRC DST' expecting exactly two words. It offers ready-made checks such as 'no extra words allowed', 'at least N words', 'exactly N words', 'a range of N to M words', 'only words from an approved list', 'no repeated words', and a way to combine several checks together. A command author attaches one of these (or a custom function with the same shape) to a command, and the framework calls it automatically before the command runs, producing a clear error message if it fails.

entrypoints.name: PositionalArgs
entrypoints.plain: The shape every argument-count validator must have: given a command and its arguments, return an error or nil.

entrypoints.name: legacyArgs
entrypoints.plain: The default (backward-compatible) argument check cobra applies when a command sets no explicit rule.

entrypoints.name: NoArgs
entrypoints.plain: Reject any positional arguments at all.

entrypoints.name: OnlyValidArgs
entrypoints.plain: Require every argument to be in the command's declared list of valid words.

entrypoints.name: NoDuplicateArgs
entrypoints.plain: Reject repeated arguments.

entrypoints.name: ArbitraryArgs
entrypoints.plain: Accept any arguments at all, no checking.

entrypoints.name: MinimumNArgs
entrypoints.plain: Require at least N arguments.

entrypoints.name: MaximumNArgs
entrypoints.plain: Require at most N arguments.

entrypoints.name: ExactArgs
entrypoints.plain: Require exactly N arguments.

entrypoints.name: RangeArgs
entrypoints.plain: Require between min and max arguments.

entrypoints.name: MatchAll
entrypoints.plain: Combine several of these checks into one that requires all of them to pass.

entrypoints.name: ExactValidArgs
entrypoints.plain: Require exactly N arguments, all drawn from the valid-args list.

units.name: flag-groups
units.role: Enforce declared relationships between a command's flags (required-together, one-required, mutually-exclusive).
units.description: This code lets a command-line tool declare rules about how its flags (options) relate to each other — for example 'these three flags must all be used together', 'at least one of these flags must be given', or 'these flags cannot be used at the same time'. It stores those rules as tags on the flags themselves, then checks the rules right before a command runs (and also adjusts what the shell's tab-completion suggests) so users get a clear error message if they violate the rule instead of the program behaving unpredictably.

entrypoints.name: (*Command).MarkFlagsMutuallyExclusive

entrypoints.name: (*Command).ValidateFlagGroups
entrypoints.plain: Check the current flags against every declared rule, producing an error if one is broken.

entrypoints.name: (*Command).enforceFlagGroupsForCompletion

units.name: completion-engine
units.role: Compute what a shell should offer as tab-completion for a partially-typed command line, independent of any one shell's syntax.
units.description: This is the brain behind shell tab-completion: it figures out what a program should suggest when a user presses Tab on a partial command line. It walks the command tree, matches flags and subcommands, calls any custom completion function a program author registered for a specific flag, checks 'active help' hint messages, and formats the answer as a simple text protocol along with debug logging controlled by environment variables. It also provides the small helper methods programs use to mark a flag as filename-only, directory-only, or custom-completed. Translating this protocol's answer into actual bash/zsh/fish/PowerShell script syntax is a separate job handled by the per-shell generator units.

units.name: bash-completion-gen
units.role: Serialize a command tree into a legacy (v1) static Bash completion script.
units.description: This is one of several 'translators' that turn cobra's knowledge of a program's commands and flags into a working shell script for a specific shell — in this case, the older, static style of Bash completion. It walks the whole tree of commands and sub-commands and writes out a chunk of Bash scripting logic listing each one's name, flags, and required arguments up front, so Bash can offer Tab suggestions without calling back into the running program. It can hand back the generated script as text or save it straight to a file.

entrypoints.name: (*Command).GenBashCompletionFile

effects.description: GenBashCompletionFile calls os.Create(filename) to write the generated script to disk.

The generated Bash script text (not this Go code) reads $BASH_COMP_DEBUG_FILE and appends debug lines to it, and uses eval to re-invoke the host program at completion time — that execution happens later, in the user's shell.

units.name: bash-completion-v2-gen
units.role: Serialize a command tree into a modern (v2) dynamic Bash completion script.
units.description: This is the modern replacement for the legacy Bash completion translator: instead of hard-coding a static list of flags and commands into the shell script, it writes a smarter Bash script that calls back into the running program itself at Tab-press time to ask what's valid right now, including active-help hint messages. It can hand back the generated script as text or save it straight to a file, and it is what cobra's own built-in 'completion bash' subcommand uses.

entrypoints.name: (*Command).GenBashCompletionV2
entrypoints.plain: Write the modern Bash completion script for this command to a writer.

entrypoints.name: (*Command).GenBashCompletionFileV2
entrypoints.plain: Write the modern Bash completion script for this command to a file.

effects.description: GenBashCompletionFileV2 calls os.Create(filename) to write the generated script to disk.

The generated Bash script text itself later performs shell-level I/O (reads $BASH_COMP_DEBUG_FILE, evals a call back into the host program) when sourced by a user's shell — not executed by this Go code.

units.name: zsh-completion-gen
units.role: Serialize a command tree into a dynamic Zsh completion script.
units.description: This translator writes out a ready-to-use Zsh (a shell) autocomplete script for a program. When a user asks for Zsh completion, it builds a chunk of Zsh-scripting text that, once installed, calls back into the program's own hidden completion command at Tab-press time to ask what's valid, including active-help hint messages. It can hand back the script as text or save it straight to a file.

units.name: doc-generators
units.role: Render a command tree into static documentation files (man, Markdown, ReST, YAML).
units.description: This is the documentation toolkit: given the tree of commands and flags that make up a command-line program, it produces ready-to-publish documentation in four common formats — Unix man pages, Markdown, reStructuredText, and YAML. It walks the command tree, pulling out each command's name, description, usage examples, and flags, and either writes the result to a stream the caller supplies or creates one file per command in a target directory. It knows what documentation for a command should contain and how to format it in each style, but nothing about how commands are defined or executed — that comes from the library it renders.

man_docs.go, md_docs.go, and rest_docs.go call time.Now() to stamp the generated document's date.

violations_observed.note: The shell-agnostic completion engine reads annotation-key constants that are defined in bash_completions.go (the legacy v1 Bash generator), even though the annotations themselves are shell-agnostic in meaning and used by every shell generator. This is a historical naming/ownership leak: completion-engine should own this shared vocabulary itself rather than importing it from one specific shell's file.

bash_completions.go reads the package-private flagCompletionFunctions map and flagCompletionMutex directly instead of going through an exported accessor, reaching past completion-engine's public surface (RegisterFlagCompletionFunc/GetFlagCompletionFunc) into its internal registry.
